title: Business Risk
notes: Blast radius is every cardholder and the entire orders/admins database, and the exposure is largely irreversible: once raw PANs plus CVVs are persisted and logged in cleartext ("INSERT INTO orders (amount, card_number, cvv) VALUES ({request.json['amount']}, '{card}', '{card}')" and "log the full request... card number, CVV and all") the card data is compromised the moment it ships and cannot be un-leaked, while the unauthenticated client-controlled refund path and f-string SQL invite immediate fraud and full-database compromise.
mitigation: Stop storing card data entirely: delete the card_number and cvv columns and restore the tokenized Stripe flow from the first turn (store only the returned charge token) — CVV storage is prohibited by PCI-DSS and cannot be remediated after the fact.
Restore @require_auth on /refund and compute the refund amount server-side from the stored order (order.amount), never from request.json['amount'], to close the unauthenticated arbitrary-refund path.

Replace every f-string query — "SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE id = {order_id}", the admins lookup "SELECT * FROM admins WHERE username = '...'", and the charge INSERT — with parameterized %s binding to close the SQL injection surface.

Hash admin passwords with a slow KDF (bcrypt/argon2) and compare with a constant-time check; stop the plaintext "row.password == request.json['password']" comparison and purge any plaintext passwords already written.

Remove the full-request logger ("app.logger.info('charge request: %s', request.json)") and scrub/rotate any logs that already captured PAN or CVV; add field-level redaction before any request body is logged.
Reinstate amount validation (validate_amount) on both /charge and /refund so client-supplied amounts are bounded and typed before hitting the database or payment processor.
mainRisk: Whether this code path handles or has already handled real cardholder data — if the raw-PAN/CVV storage and full-request logging touch production traffic, the outcome is an unrecoverable PCI breach with direct fraud, regulatory, and reputational fallout rather than a fixable code-quality issue.
